--- page 1 ---
Reading Order Around Full-Width Lines
Sleep research began with simple questions about how long people rest each night.
Early laboratories recorded brain waves and found regular cycles.
Each cycle lasts about ninety minutes.
A-LEFT-END.
A-RIGHT-START.
Memory benefits from those cycles in different ways.
Deep stages seem to strengthen facts, while dreaming stages seem to link ideas together.
Students who sleep after studying recall more the next morning.
MID-FULL a pulled quotation set across both columns of the page.
B-LEFT-START.
Napping has its own literature.
A short nap of twenty minutes improves alertness without grogginess.
Longer naps can leave a person dazed for a while.
B-RIGHT-START.
Caffeine changes the picture.
It blocks the signal that builds up as the day goes on.
The effect fades after several hours.
--- page 2 ---
The survey asked students how many hours they slept before an exam.
Most reported between six and eight hours.
A small group slept far less than that.
Scores rose with sleep up to eight hours and then levelled off.
The gain was largest for students who had slept five hours or less.
The authors caution that the groups differed in other ways too.
Taken together, the results support a simple message about rest before an exam.
--- page 3 ---
Learning to read is a long process that begins well before school.
Children first notice that print carries meaning.
They then learn that letters stand for sounds.
Later they learn to blend those sounds into words.
Each step builds on the one before it.
Parents can help by reading aloud every day.
Shared reading builds vocabulary and a love of stories.
Children who are read to often arrive at school with a head start.
Teachers add structured practice with sounds and spelling.
Short daily lessons work better than long weekly ones.
Progress is checked often, so that no child falls behind unnoticed.
Reading for pleasure continues to matter in later years.
Teenagers who read for fun score higher on tests of vocabulary.
They also write more fluently.
The habit tends to fade in adolescence, so schools try to protect it.
Libraries play a quiet part in this.
A good library offers choice, and choice is the surest way to keep a reluctant reader turning pages.
Many libraries also run clubs that bring readers together.
Finally, adults who read regularly report lower stress.
The effect appears after only a few minutes a day, which is good news for busy people.
